passages.title: Breadth or Depth in the School Curriculum?
passages.subtitle: Should teenagers study a wide range of subjects or focus early on one area?
paragraphs: When planning a national school curriculum, education leaders must make an important decision: should teenagers study many different subjects, or should they focus deeply on just a few? Different countries answer this question in very different ways, and each system has its own strengths and weaknesses.

In countries like England, students aged 16 typically specialise in only three or four subjects for their final two years of high school, known as A-levels. Supporters of this narrow approach argue that it allows students to gain in-depth knowledge of the subjects they love most. It also prepares them well for specific university courses such as medicine or architecture, where strong early training is helpful.

By contrast, countries such as the United States, France, and Japan prefer a broad model. Teenagers continue studying core subjects like mathematics, literature, and foreign languages alongside science, history, and arts right up until they finish school at 18. Educators who support this model believe it provides a well-rounded education and keeps career choices open for longer, since many 16-year-olds do not yet know what job they want.

Within this debate, there is also disagreement over which subjects deserve the most classroom hours. Many governments strongly promote science and technology subjects because they see them as engines of economic growth. As a result, subjects such as history, art, and music sometimes receive less funding and fewer teaching hours.

However, historians and artists warn that cutting creative and cultural subjects is a mistake. History teaches young people how societies change and helps them think critically about news and politics. Meanwhile, art and music encourage imagination and design thinking—qualities that even top technology companies look for when creating new products.

Today, a growing number of international schools use programmes like the International Baccalaureate (IB), which asks students to study six subjects across both sciences and humanities, with three at a higher level and three at a standard level. Many teachers see this as a smart way to offer both breadth and depth.

passages.title: Compulsory Schooling and School Dropouts
passages.subtitle: Can raising the school-leaving age keep vulnerable teenagers in education?
paragraphs: In the past, many teenagers left school at 14 or 16 to work in factories or on farms. Today, however, unskilled jobs are disappearing, and several countries have raised the legal school-leaving age to 18. Governments hope that keeping young people in education for longer will reduce unemployment and improve social mobility, giving children from poorer families a better chance to earn higher incomes as adults.

Despite these laws, dropping out of school remains a serious problem worldwide. Before students formally leave school, they often show early warning signs, such as regular truancy—missing classes without permission—and falling grades. Research shows that teenagers from vulnerable backgrounds, including those dealing with family poverty, bullying, or learning difficulties, are much more likely to leave school without basic qualifications.

Leaving school early can have long-lasting effects. One major consequence is low adult literacy. Adults who struggle to read contracts, fill out job applications, or understand medical instructions face daily challenges and often get stuck in temporary, low-paid work. In addition, countries with high dropout rates spend more public money on welfare support.

Simply forcing unhappy teenagers to sit in academic classrooms until age 18 does not always work. Teachers report that when students feel bored or behind in lessons, they may disrupt the class or stop attending altogether. Therefore, many education experts argue that raising the school-leaving age only succeeds if schools offer flexible choices.

One effective solution is creating a strong vocational pathway from age 16. Instead of studying only academic textbooks, teenagers can stay in education by training to become chefs, electricians, or computer technicians. In the Netherlands, a national programme also tracks absences daily. When a student misses school without a valid reason, a local counsellor contacts the family quickly to offer support rather than punishment.

For people who have already left school early, second-chance learning is equally important. Community centres and evening colleges now run free adult literacy classes and online certificate courses. By helping both teenagers and adults return to learning, societies can ensure that an early mistake does not close the door to a better future.

passages.title: Teaching Life Skills in Schools
passages.subtitle: Why practical lessons in finance, community service, and parenting matter
paragraphs: Ask most adults what they wish they had learned at school, and few will say more algebra. Instead, many complain that they left school knowing how to pass exams, yet having no idea how to manage a bank account, pay taxes, or cook a healthy meal. Because of this gap, there is growing support for adding practical life skills to the standard school timetable.

One of the most widely recommended subjects is financial literacy. Young adults today face easy access to credit cards, online shopping, and student loans, which can quickly lead to debt if they are not careful. Teaching teenagers how to make a monthly budget, understand interest rates, and save for emergencies can prevent serious financial mistakes later in life.

Beyond money management, many educators believe schools should also teach civic responsibility through community service. In countries such as Canada and Singapore, high school students are required to complete a set number of volunteer hours—such as helping elderly neighbours, planting trees, or assisting at local food banks—before graduating. Supporters argue that these hands-on experiences are excellent for character building, teaching empathy and teamwork in a way that textbooks cannot.

Some experts even suggest introducing basic parenting skills and relationship classes for older teenagers. Since most young people will one day raise children or care for family members, learning about child nutrition, communication, and patience could strengthen future families. Critics, however, feel that parenting is a private matter that should be learned at home rather than taught by school teachers.

Indeed, adding life skills to schools is not without challenges. Teachers already have crowded schedules and strict national tests to prepare for. If schools add new lessons on cooking, finance, and volunteering, some parents worry there will be less time left for reading, maths, and science. Furthermore, teachers themselves may need extra training to teach financial or practical topics accurately.

In my view, schools do not need to replace academic subjects with life skills; rather, they can weave them together. Maths classes can include real-life budgeting problems, while one afternoon a month can be dedicated to local volunteering. Preparing students for exams is important, but preparing them to live independent, responsible adult lives is the true purpose of education.
